overview.description: Calculation (also known as Strategy or 'Broken Intervals') is a unique solitaire card game that deviates from standard 'Klondike' mechanics. Unlike most solitaires that build in simple 1-2-3 steps, each of the four foundation piles in Calculation builds at a different mathematical interval: Pile 1 goes 1, 2, 3...; Pile 2 goes 2, 4, 6...; Pile 3 goes 3, 6, 9...; and Pile 4 goes 4, 8, Q... It is a game of pure skill and memory where the layout of the 'Waste' piles determines victory.

history.origins: Developed as a mental exercise in the early 20th century. It was popularized by the legendary card experts Albert H. Morehead and Geoffrey Mott-Smith in their seminal book 'The Complete Book of Solitaire'.
timeline: 1949: Rules are first published in major US card game encyclopedias.
1980s: Becomes a standard 'Expert Level' solitaire in early digital card game collections.
Present: Highly regarded by mathematicians and puzzle enthusiasts for its lack of 'luck' once the deck is shuffled.
21st Century: Popularized on mobile platforms as 'Strategy Solitaire'.
history.evolution: The game was refined from a chaotic multi-deck version into the elegant single-deck 4-pile variant known today.
history.cultural: Associated with 'Analytical Patience'â€”playing the game is seen as a way to sharpen arithmetic skills.

setup.players: One player (solitaire). The game is played by a single player who turns cards from the stock and builds the four foundations or places cards on the four waste (tableau) piles.
setup.deck: 52 cards. Remove one Ace, one 2, one 3, and one 4. Place them as the base of 4 Foundation piles.
setup.dealing: Remove one A, 2, 3, 4; place as base of four foundations. Rest form stock. Turn from stock to foundation or waste.

rules.objective: Move all 52 cards onto the four foundation piles by building each foundation in its fixed interval sequence (Ace+1, 2+2, 3+3, 4+4) until every card is played; the game is lost if no further play is possible.
rules.gameplay:
1. Turn up a card from the Stock.
2. If it can be played on a Foundation, do so.
3. If not, you MUST place it on one of the 4 Waste piles.
4. You can only move the TOP card of a Waste pile to a Foundation. You cannot move cards between Waste piles.
keyRules: Four foundations build by intervals: +1, +2, +3, +4. Only top of waste movable to foundation.

strategy.basic: Keep your Kings at the bottom of the Waste piles! Since every foundation ends with a King, a King is the 'Deadest' card in the game. If you place a King on top of a 5, that 5 is lost until the King is cleared (which can only happen at the very end).
strategy.intermediate: Waste Pile Organization: Dedicate each of the 4 Waste piles to specific card sequences or values. For example, use Pile 1 for high cards (J, Q, K), Pile 2 for mid-cards, and Piles 3 and 4 for sequences that match the Foundations' intervals. If you see a card that is needed soon in the 'Steps of 3' foundation, put it in a dedicated pile.
strategy.advanced: Look-Ahead Calculation: Memorize the next 3-4 cards needed for EACH foundation. If you draw a 6, and Pile 3 (Step of 3) currently has a 3 on it, you can play the 6. But if Pile 3 has a 9, and the 6 is needed much later, decide if it's better to bury the 6 or keep it accessible.
tips: The 'Step of 4' sequence (4, 8, Q, 3...) is usually the hardest to remember. Practice reciting it before playing.
Never block a lower-value card with a higher-value one in a Waste pile unless you have no other choice.

play_card.description: Play the turned card onto a foundation if it is the next in that foundation's interval sequence (Pile 1: +1, Pile 2: +2, Pile 3: +3, Pile 4: +4), or place it on one of the four waste piles. Only the top card of a waste pile may be moved to a foundation.
play_card.constraints: Card from stock must go to a foundation if legal, otherwise must be placed on one of four waste piles; only the top card of a waste pile may move to a foundation; cards cannot move between waste piles.

engine.deckDescription: A standard 52-card French deck comprising four suits: Hearts, Diamonds, Clubs, and Spades. Each suit contains thirteen ranks: Ace, 2 through 10, Jack, Queen, and King, providing versatile options for various card games.
engine.suitDescription: Four traditional French suits: Hearts (Cœur), Diamonds (Carreau), Clubs (Trèfle), and Spades (Pique), each represented with standard French card iconography and distinct color coding for easy identification.
engine.rankDescription: Standard thirteen ranks per suit: Ace, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, Jack, Queen, and King, where each rank has distinct value and meaning depending on the specific game rules and player strategies.
